catalog_locator: ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.4 Tone, pp. 28-30; sec. 2.6 (loanwords) p. 39
catalog_quote: Tone is distinctive in Logba. Two tones are identified in the lexical data compiled on Logba. High tone is marked ( ́) and Low tone is unmarked. A third tone, Rising tone is phonetically realised on a single syllable peak and is represented as ( ̌). This tone is found on a limited number of borrowed words from Ewe with the inland Ewe dialect tone (see 82). Tone is realised on vowels and syllabic nasals. The meaning of a word depends on the tone of each syllable as well as the vowels and consonants of which the word is made. ... Monosyllabic words can either be Low tone or High tone. ... All possible tonal patterns, LL, HH, LH, and HL, are attested in disyllabic roots. ... English is a stress-timed language and has syllable types which are not found in the Logba language. Glottolog lists no competing grammar (the 1953 Dorvlo entry is a mis-dated duplicate; Westermann 1903 is an 18-pp sketch). sources.citation: Shluinsky, Andrey. 2024. Review of: Jason Kandybowicz, Bertille Baron, Philip T. Duncan & Hironori Katsuda, Ikpana interrogatives (OUP 2023). Linguistique et langues africaines. DOI 10.4000/13lt7 (OpenEdition, open access).
sources.quote: web lookups-extracted: 'Ikpana, like other Kwa languages (and most West African languages), has lexical tones (three level tones, which is typical for GTM).' Ch. 4 reports controlled production experiments with pitch tracks: interrogatives end higher than declaratives, declaratives show downstep/upstep and H/M 'tone reversal', yes/no questions show final vowel lengthening. No mention of word stress or accent.
